reading.title: Small Parts That Change a Word
reading.purpose: See how three short prefixes change the meaning of everyday base words.
paras: A prefix is a small part added to the front of a word. Just three letters at the start can flip what a word means or move it back in time.

The prefix dis- often means "not" or "the opposite of." A dishonest person does not tell the truth. If you disobey a rule, you do not follow it. When you disconnect a hose from a tap, you pull the two parts apart. If a friend breaks a vow twice, you may distrust them and stop relying on their word.

The prefix mis- means "wrongly" or "badly." A bad sign can mislead hikers and send them down the wrong path. To mistreat a pet is to be unkind or rough with it. Almost everyone will misplace a book or a hat now and then, putting it where they cannot find it.

The prefix pre- means "before." A cook will preheat an oven so it is warm before muffins go in. A film preview gives you a quick look before the full show starts. Scientists dig up prehistoric bones from long before people wrote down records.
Once you know dis-, mis-, and pre-, you can read many new words on your own.

choices: to give a borrowed book back to the library before it is due
to put something where you cannot find it
to hide a friend's hat on purpose during a game
to clean up a messy room before dinner time
qs.why: Paragraph 3 explains that when you misplace something, you put it where you cannot find it.

qs.q: Which sentence shows how the prefix pre- is used in cooking?
choices: A film preview gives you a quick look before the full show starts.
A cook will preheat an oven so it is warm before muffins go in.
Scientists dig up prehistoric bones from long before people wrote down records.
qs.why: This sentence shows a cook warming an oven before baking muffins.

ev.text: A cook will preheat an oven so it is warm before muffins go in.

qs.q: Why might someone begin to distrust a friend?
choices: The friend disconnected a garden hose from the tap after watering flowers.
The friend forgot where a favorite book was left last week at school.
The friend broke a vow more than once.
The friend warmed up the kitchen oven before baking muffins for lunch.
qs.why: Paragraph 2 says that if a friend breaks a vow twice, you may distrust them.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Knowing prefixes like dis-, mis-, and pre- helps you read new words.
Cooks and scientists use prefixes far more often than hikers or pet owners do.
Every English word needs a three-letter prefix at the start to make sense.
Prefixes always turn a friendly word into an opposite or unkind word.
qs.why: Each paragraph teaches one prefix with examples, and the closing sentence explains that these prefixes help you read new words.

clues.text: be unkind or rough with it
from long before people wrote down records
